**(e) NEW DEFECT the dossier misses - the five alarms will most likely NOT self-heal**

The dossier says the five `treat_missing_data = "breaching"` alarms "will resolve themselves the
moment metrics start flowing." **I do not believe they will**, and the reason is in the repo.

The alarms specify these dimension sets:

| Alarm | file:line | `dimensions` |
|---|---|---|
| `cpu-high` | `monitoring/main.tf:376-378` | `{ InstanceId }` |
| `mem-high` | `:401-403` | `{ InstanceId }` |
| `disk-root-high` | `:426-429` | `{ InstanceId, path = "/" }` |
| `disk-data-high` | `:452-455` | `{ InstanceId, path = "/var/lib/postgresql" }` |
| `inode-low-*` (x2, `for_each`) | `:1643-1646` | `{ InstanceId, path = each.key }` |

The agent config will publish with:

- `append_dimensions = {InstanceId, InstanceType}` (`bootstrap-ec2.sh:979-982`) on **every** metric;
- plus the cpu plugin's own `cpu` tag (`totalcpu: true` -> `cpu=cpu-total`);
- plus the disk plugin's own `path`, `device`, `fstype` tags (no `drop_device` set).

So the published metrics carry `{InstanceId, InstanceType, cpu}`, `{InstanceId, InstanceType}`, and
`{InstanceId, InstanceType, path, device, fstype}` respectively. **A CloudWatch alarm matches an
exact dimension set - it cannot match a subset.** None of the five alarms' dimension sets exist
as published metrics, so all five stay `INSUFFICIENT_DATA`, and with `treat_missing_data =
"breaching"` that renders as ALARM. Forever. Even with a perfectly healthy agent.

The Terraform author was aware of the extra dimensions and reasoned about them incorrectly -
`monitoring/main.tf:1641-1642` says, verbatim:

> `# Match the disk_used_percent alarm dimensions: InstanceId + path. The CW`
> `# Agent also emits device + fstype but those add fragility (a remount`
> `# changes them) for no extra precision in our single-instance design.`

That is a decision to *omit* dimensions the agent emits - which does not produce a looser match,
it produces **no match at all**. [V for the config and the alarm dimensions; **[I]** for the
conclusion, because it rests on (1) the agent publishing no aggregated rollup when
`aggregation_dimensions` is absent, and (2) CloudWatch alarm dimension matching being exact.
Both are standard behaviour but I could not confirm them against the live account.]

**Why this matters for B1 specifically.** It changes the sequencing contract with B6. The dossier
says "fix B1 and B2 first, then subscribe." If this finding holds, subscribing after B1+B2 still
delivers five permanently-ALARM emails to a freshly-confirmed mailbox on day one - the exact
alarm-fatigue outcome B6 exists to prevent. **The gate on B6 must be a measured dimension check,
not the mere fact that B1 landed.** That check is one read-only call and is in my verification
plan (I8). The fix itself is out of my lane (Terraform alarms, or an `aggregation_dimensions`
key in §14) - see I10 and I11.

**(g) Cost - what shipping these log groups actually costs**

Retention is **14 days** on dev (`app/dev.tfvars:23`). The honest arithmetic:

```
monthly = (GB_ingested_per_month * ingest_$/GB)
        + (avg_GB_stored * storage_$/GB-month)
        + (KMS GenerateDataKey requests / 10,000 * $0.03)
```

- **Ingestion dominates.** `~$0.50-0.63/GB` in eu-central-1 [I - I could not hit the pricing API].
- **Volume estimate for dev** [I]: nginx-access ~10-20 MB/day (E1's JSON format roughly doubles
  line size, ~200 -> ~400 B, which is the dossier's own `$1.30/env/month` figure); the Docker
  JSON `app` group is the wildcard at ~50-200 MB/day under active use (note `uvicorn.access` is
  pinned to `WARNING` at `backend/app/main.py:54`, so there are no per-request lines); postgres
  5-20 MB/day; auth.log 5-50 MB/day on a public EIP; `/var/log/audit/audit.log` is the real
  unknown - auditd can be very loud depending on the installed ruleset and is worth measuring
  on day one. **Band: 0.1-1 GB/day -> 3-30 GB/month -> roughly $2-$20/month.**
- **Storage is negligible.** 14 days retained, stored compressed, at `$0.03/GB-month`: on the
  order of `$0.01-0.05/month`.
- **KMS adds ~$0.20/month.** CW Logs caches data keys, so roughly one `GenerateDataKey` per group
  per 5 minutes: `7 x 288 x 30 = ~60k requests` at `$0.03/10k`. [I]

**Correction to the brief's framing.** Retention does **not** bound this bill in any meaningful
way - it bounds *storage*, which is under 5% of it. **The only levers on ingestion are the
`collect_list` contents and per-source verbosity.** If cost becomes a concern the actions are:
drop `letsencrypt` (near-zero value, tiny anyway), reduce auditd rules, or - the real one -
measure `IncomingBytes` per group for a week and then decide. Do not lower retention expecting
a saving.

Total: **on the order of $3-$25/month for dev**, with the honest caveat that the range is wide
because nothing has ever been measured. The very first thing the fix produces is the data
needed to replace this estimate with a number.

---

##### I5. The complete fix

Three changes, all in `infra/scripts/bootstrap-ec2.sh` §14, plus the host-side application.
This covers **B1 only**. B2 (permissions), B3 (stream collision), B4 (collect the agent log)
and B5 (exit-status check) are separate edits to the same section - see I10 for how they compose.

**Design decision: relocate the sink, do not pre-create it in `/var/log`.**
The agent's vendor-default log path is inside its own installation tree, which the agent's
own tooling owns. Putting the sink there means cwagent owns the *directory*, so `open()` and
`rename()` (rotation) both work, no logrotate stanza is ever needed or tempting, and the setup
step is `install -d` (idempotent) instead of `install <file>` (destructive on re-run). One
extra line buys the removal of all three latent regressions from I3.

---

**Step 1 - fix the stale section reference at `bootstrap-ec2.sh:341`.**

Find (line 341, inside the §8 ACL comment):

```bash
# because the cwagent user may not exist yet — repeated after cwagent install
# in §13.
```

Replace with:

```bash
# because the cwagent user may not exist yet — repeated after cwagent install
# in §14.
```

*Why:* the repeat is at `:951-952`, which is §14. A wrong cross-reference in the one comment
that explains the ordering contract is the kind of thing that makes the next person put an
`install -o cwagent` in the wrong place.

---

**Step 2 - assert the `cwagent` user exists and own the agent's log directory.**

Find, at `bootstrap-ec2.sh:948-952` (the existing block, immediately after the `dpkg` guard):

```bash
# Re-grant ACL now that cwagent user exists. See §8 above for why o::r is
# load-bearing (preserves world-read on per-container /etc/hosts so non-
# root containers can do DNS).
setfacl -R -m u:cwagent:rX,o::r /var/lib/docker/containers
setfacl -R -d -m u:cwagent:rX,o::r /var/lib/docker/containers
```

Replace with:

```bash
# The agent's deb postinst creates the `cwagent` user. Everything below
# depends on that; assert it explicitly so a packaging change fails with a
# named error instead of `install: invalid user 'cwagent'` buried 1,200
# lines into the bootstrap log.
getent passwd cwagent >/dev/null || {
    echo "[bootstrap] FATAL: user 'cwagent' does not exist after installing amazon-cloudwatch-agent" >&2
    exit 1
}

# Re-grant ACL now that cwagent user exists. See §8 above for why o::r is
# load-bearing (preserves world-read on per-container /etc/hosts so non-
# root containers can do DNS).
setfacl -R -m u:cwagent:rX,o::r /var/lib/docker/containers
setfacl -R -d -m u:cwagent:rX,o::r /var/lib/docker/containers

# The agent runs as `cwagent` (run_as_user below) and constructs its telemetry
# logger BEFORE doing any work — if it cannot open its own log sink it exits 1
# and ships nothing at all, forever, with no external signal. /var/log is
# root-owned, so a sink there requires a pre-created root-blessed file AND a
# logrotate stanza with explicit `create 0644 cwagent cwagent`, AND breaks the
# agent's own size-based rotation (rename needs write on the directory).
# Keeping the sink inside the agent's own tree removes all three problems:
# cwagent owns the directory, so open() and rotation both work forever, and
# nothing else in /var/log is tempted to manage it.
# `install -d` is idempotent and never truncates — safe under a reconcile
# re-run (unlike `install /dev/null <file>`, which would wipe the live log).
install -d -o cwagent -g cwagent -m 0755 /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/logs
```

---

**Step 3 - point the agent's `logfile` at the now-owned directory.**

Find, at `bootstrap-ec2.sh:964-968` (inside the unquoted heredoc):

```
  "agent": {
    "metrics_collection_interval": 60,
    "logfile": "/var/log/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.log",
    "run_as_user": "cwagent"
  },
```

Replace with:

```
  "agent": {
    "metrics_collection_interval": 60,
    "logfile": "/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/logs/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.log",
    "run_as_user": "cwagent"
  },
```

*Why this and not `run_as_user: root`:* running the whole log-shipping daemon as root to avoid a
directory-ownership problem widens the blast radius of a process that tails eight files and
holds an IAM credential, for zero benefit. *Why this and not omitting `logfile` entirely:* the
default would probably resolve to the same path, but "probably" is not a property you want in
the line whose failure mode is total silence. Setting it explicitly, next to an explicit
`install -d` of the same directory, makes the contract self-evident and independent of what the
`-ctl` wrapper does.

**Heredoc note (load-bearing):** the new path contains no `$`, no backtick and no backslash, so
it survives the unquoted `<<EOF` at `:962` byte-for-byte. Verify with the render command in I8
rather than by eye.

---

**Nothing to delete (INV-3/INV-12).** `/var/log/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.log` does not exist on
the box - the agent has never been able to create it [V, dossier]. There is no superseded code
path, no second config, and no dual implementation. The change is a one-line path move plus a
one-line directory create; the old path simply ceases to be referenced anywhere in the tree
(`grep -rn '/var/log/amazon-cloudwatch-agent' infra/ docs/` must return only the
`docs/SIMPLE_AWS_DEPLOYMENT.md:1219` design-doc copy - see the doc note below).

**Documentation (same commit).** `docs/SIMPLE_AWS_DEPLOYMENT.md:1219` carries the same
`"logfile": "/var/log/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.log"` in the §10.1 reference config that
`bootstrap-ec2.sh` was materialized from. Update it in lockstep with a one-line note, or the
next person who regenerates the script from the doc reintroduces the bug. This is a doc-only
edit with no runtime effect.

---

**Step 4 - apply to the running box (the half that evaporates).**

The repo edit reaches `s3://velocityai-dev-pg-dumps-577954642302/config/bootstrap-ec2.sh` on the
next dev push - `infra/terraform/app/main.tf:79-94` declares `aws_s3_object.bootstrap_script`
with `source_hash = filemd5(...)`, and `infra/buildspec.yml:203` runs `$TF/app apply` on every
build [V]. But **nothing on the dev box ever re-reads it** (C1): dev's userData has no
firstboot service and `/var/lib/velocityai/.bootstrap-done` does not exist. So the running
instance needs a scoped, one-shot application.

```bash
set -euo pipefail
DEV=i-092d5961f5aca87a6
NAME=$(aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids "$DEV" \
  --query 'Reservations[0].Instances[0].Tags[?Key==`Name`].Value|[0]' --output text)
[ "$NAME" = "velocityai-dev-app" ] || { echo "REFUSING: $DEV is '$NAME'"; exit 1; }

aws ssm send-command --instance-ids "$DEV" --document-name AWS-RunShellScript \
  --comment "B1: relocate cwagent log sink to a cwagent-owned dir" \
  --parameters 'commands=[
    "set -euo pipefail",
    "TS=$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)",
    "install -d -m 0700 /root/cwagent-backup-$TS",
    "cp -a /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json /root/cwagent-backup-$TS/ 2>/dev/null || true",
    "cp -a /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.d/file_amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json /root/cwagent-backup-$TS/ 2>/dev/null || true",
    "getent passwd cwagent >/dev/null || { echo FATAL: no cwagent user >&2; exit 1; }",
    "install -d -o cwagent -g cwagent -m 0755 /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/logs",
    "python3 - <<PY",
    "import json,pathlib",
    "p=pathlib.Path(\"/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json\")",
    "d=json.loads(p.read_text())",
    "d[\"agent\"][\"logfile\"]=\"/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/logs/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.log\"",
    "p.write_text(json.dumps(d,indent=2)+\"\\n\")",
    "PY",
    "/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl -a fetch-config -m ec2 -s -c file:/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json",
    "sleep 10",
    "/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl -m ec2 -a status"
  ]' --output text
```

Two details that are not cosmetic:

- **`--instance-ids`, never `--targets`.** `Project`/`Owner`/`CostCenter`/`Repo`/`ManagedBy`/`Component`
  are byte-identical across dev, stage and prod [V, dossier Appendix 2]. A tag-targeted
  `send-command` would hit all three. The `Name` pre-flight makes the instance id
  self-verifying.
- **The Python rewrite, not `sed`.** The on-box JSON is a *rendered* file (interpolations already
  resolved); a JSON load/modify/dump cannot corrupt it the way an unanchored `sed` on a path
  containing `/` can, and it fails loudly if the file is not the shape we expect.

**Durability of each half:** the repo edit is durable and reaches S3 on the next dev push, but
**only regenerates host state if someone re-runs the script**. The SSM application is
immediately effective and survives reboot (root EBS) and `docker compose pull` (nginx and the
agent are host-installed), but is **lost on instance replacement** (`delete_on_termination=true`,
zero snapshots). Both halves are required; neither is sufficient.

---

##### I6. Ripple-effect analysis - why nothing else breaks

*Assume the fix is wrong. Where does it hurt?*

- **The agent starts and immediately floods a group with a backlog.** The tailers start at the
  *end* of each file by default for a first-time state, so there is no historical replay of
  months of nginx logs. If the agent did start from byte 0 on eight files the first-minute
  ingestion spike would be bounded by current file sizes on a 60 GB root volume at 32% used
  [V, dossier] - tens of MB, one-off, a few cents. Not a risk worth gating on, but worth
  watching `IncomingBytes` for the first hour.
- **The agent starts, and B2 has not landed.** Then it runs, opens its own log successfully, and
  logs a permission-denied line **per configured file, repeatedly**. That is the intended
  outcome - it is exactly how B2 becomes visible instead of silent - but it means B1 alone
  produces a noisy `system` group. It also means **B1 must not be shipped and then left**: the
  window between B1 and B2 is the only window where the agent writes mostly errors. Ship them
  together (I10).
- **Feedback loop from collecting the agent's own log (B4).** The agent tailing its own log is
  the classic amplification worry. It does not amplify here: the tailer records position in its
  state directory and does not log per shipped line, so one error line produces one shipped
  event, not N. The genuinely dangerous variant is "agent logs an error about shipping its own
  log", which would loop - but that requires the agent's own log destination to be broken while
  the agent is otherwise healthy, and B1+B2 remove exactly that condition. Worth one look at
  `IncomingBytes` on `/velocityai/dev/system` in the first hour anyway.
- **Concurrency / ordering inside bootstrap.** `install -d` at the new position runs after
  `dpkg -i` (`:945`) and after the `getent` assertion, and before the `cat >` heredoc (`:962`)
  and before `fetch-config` (`:1005`). Nothing between those points touches
  `/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent`. Under `set -euo pipefail` a failure at any of the three
  new lines aborts the script - which is correct: sections 15-20 (deploy user, backups, systemd
  units, app start) all depend on a coherent host, and silently continuing is what produced
  this bug in the first place.
- **Startup/shutdown and reboot.** `install -d` is not order-sensitive relative to systemd; the
  agent unit is package-enabled and starts on boot, finds an existing cwagent-owned directory,
  and opens its sink. On a re-run of the whole script, `install -d` re-applies mode/ownership
  and the config `cat >` overwrites identically - no divergence.
- **Partial application.** If the SSM command dies after `install -d` but before the config
  rewrite: harmless (an empty owned directory). If it dies after the config rewrite but before
  `fetch-config`: the on-disk JSON says the new path but the running (crash-looping) agent still
  uses the old translated TOML - i.e. exactly today's state, no worse. If it dies after
  `fetch-config`: the fix is applied. **Every intermediate state is either today's behaviour or
  the fixed behaviour.** There is no state in which the fix makes things worse.
- **The shared-script hazard (the one real cross-environment risk).** `bootstrap-ec2.sh` is one
  file used by dev, stage and prod. The dev-only scope fence holds for *application*
  (`--instance-ids i-092d...` only), but the **repo edit is inherently shared** - it lands in
  every environment's S3 copy on that environment's next build, and takes effect on any future
  instance replacement in stage or prod. That is desirable (stage and prod have the identical
  bug) but it must be stated, not discovered. The change is strictly safer everywhere:
  `install -d` is idempotent, and the relocated path is the vendor default.
- **Does anything read `/var/log/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.log`?** No. It does not exist on the
  box [V, dossier], nothing in the repo references it except the config line being changed and
  the design doc, and it is not in the `collect_list` (machine-verified). Moving it strands
  nothing.
- **Unattended reboot at 04:00.** `bootstrap-ec2.sh:169-172` enables auto-reboot. A reboot
  restarts the agent, which re-opens the same sink in the same owned directory. No interaction.
- **Slow client / crashed run / fan-out / two browsers / resume.** Not applicable - this change
  is entirely host-side and touches no request path, no queue, no connection pool, and no
  in-process state. Cluster A's SSE work and this fix are disjoint at the file level.

Walking §3 of the brief item by item:

- **SC-001** (a new workflow replicates `prototype` by manifest + `AGENT.md`, zero engine edits):
  **not engaged.** No file under `backend/agents/` or `backend/app/` is touched. No workflow
  name appears anywhere in the diff.
- **INV-3 / INV-12** (no dual implementations; deleting the superseded path is part of the fix):
  **satisfied.** There is no superseded path to delete - the old sink path was never functional
  and is referenced in exactly two places, both of which this change updates
  (`bootstrap-ec2.sh:966` and `docs/SIMPLE_AWS_DEPLOYMENT.md:1219`). No second config file, no
  parallel mechanism, no fallback branch.
- **INV-13** (`deepagents` only): **not engaged.** No Python.
- **Hexagonal boundary / import-linter**: **not engaged.** No Python import moves. The baseline
  stays at exactly the one pre-existing broken contract
  (`agents.capabilities.strategies.task_loop -> agents.execution_engine.od_context ->
  app.services.od_loader`) and no second. I did not re-run `lint-imports` because the diff
  contains no `.py` file; re-running it would prove nothing this diff could have changed.
- **Q3 (additive migrations only)**: **not engaged.** No migration; the alembic chain stays at
  its current head.
- **Backward compatibility (deterministic-byte-identical `prototype`/`od_*`/PPT/code-gen)**:
  **preserved by construction.** The characterization goldens drive the engine offline with a
  scripted model and never read `infra/`. I did not run them, because a shell-script edit cannot

- **Security defaults (`exec`/`network`/`secrets`/`spawn_subagents` OFF)**: **unchanged.** No
  capability grant, no tool permission, no IAM change. The fix *narrows* nothing and *widens*

  widen the daemon's privilege.

##### I8. Test plan - fail-before / pass-after

**The honest starting point: there is no existing coverage to keep green.** No test, lint gate,
or CI step reads `infra/scripts/bootstrap-ec2.sh` [V, I2]. So the first deliverable is a gate
that would have caught this on 2026-05-11.

**New test - complete code.** Place at `backend/tests/unit/test_bootstrap_cloudwatch_agent.py`.
It follows the house idiom for repo-root resolution used by
`backend/tests/agents/test_migration_ledger.py:39` (`Path(__file__).resolve().parents[3]`).

```python
"""Offline gate on the CloudWatch-agent block of infra/scripts/bootstrap-ec2.sh (B1..B4).

The bootstrap script has ZERO automated coverage today: `infra/buildspec.yml`
pre_build runs python compileall, terraform fmt/validate, gitleaks, checkov and
trivy -- no shell syntax check and no validation of the agent config it renders.
That is why a config which has never once produced a working agent survived
2.5 months of CI.

This gate renders the §14 heredoc exactly the way bootstrap does (unquoted
`<<EOF`, so bash expands ${ENVIRONMENT} / ${ENV_TITLE} and the agent's own
\\${aws:...} placeholders survive escaped), parses the result as JSON, and
pins the four properties whose violation is silent in production:

  1. the config is valid JSON at all;
  2. the agent's telemetry sink lives in a directory the run_as_user owns --
     the B1 root cause (a sink in root-owned /var/log means the agent exits 1
     before doing any work, forever, with no external signal);
  3. the agent's own log is in the collect_list -- the B4 root cause (the
     observability system must observe itself, or its total failure produces
     no signal);
  4. every (log_group_name, log_stream_name) pair is unique -- the B3 root
     cause (two tailers on one CloudWatch stream contend for its sequence
     token and interleave).

Offline and deterministic: it shells out to bash for the render (bash is
present wherever this suite runs) and touches no network and no AWS API.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import re
import subprocess
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

# backend/tests/unit/<this file> -> repo root is parents[3]
_REPO = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[3]
_BOOTSTRAP = _REPO / "infra" / "scripts" / "bootstrap-ec2.sh"

_RUN_AS_USER_OWNED_PREFIXES = ("/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/",)


def _heredoc_body_lines() -> tuple[int, int]:
    """Return the 1-based [start, end] line range of the agent-config heredoc body.

    Located structurally (by the `cat > <path> <<EOF` opener and its `EOF`
    terminator) rather than by hardcoded line numbers, so the gate survives
    edits elsewhere in the file.
    """
    lines = _BOOTSTRAP.read_text().splitlines()
    start = None
    for i, line in enumerate(lines, start=1):
        if re.match(r"^cat > \S*amazon-cloudwatch-agent\.json <<EOF\s*$", line):
            start = i + 1
            break
    assert start is not None, "could not find the agent-config heredoc opener in bootstrap-ec2.sh"
    for j in range(start, len(lines) + 1):
        if lines[j - 1].rstrip() == "EOF":
            return start, j - 1
    raise AssertionError("agent-config heredoc has no EOF terminator")


def _render_agent_config(environment: str = "dev") -> dict:
    start, end = _heredoc_body_lines()
    body = "\n".join(_BOOTSTRAP.read_text().splitlines()[start - 1 : end])
    script = f"cat <<EOF\n{body}\nEOF\n"
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["bash", "-c", script],
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
        check=True,
        env={
            "ENVIRONMENT": environment,
            "ENV_TITLE": environment.capitalize(),
            "PATH": "/usr/bin:/bin",
        },
    ).stdout
    return json.loads(out)


def test_bootstrap_script_is_syntactically_valid():
    """`bash -n` on the whole script -- the gate that does not exist in CI today."""
    subprocess.run(["bash", "-n", str(_BOOTSTRAP)], check=True)


def test_agent_config_renders_to_valid_json():
    cfg = _render_agent_config()
    assert cfg["agent"]["run_as_user"] == "cwagent"
    assert cfg["metrics"]["namespace"] == "VelocityAI/Dev"
    # the agent's own placeholders must survive the unquoted heredoc verbatim
    assert cfg["metrics"]["append_dimensions"]["InstanceId"] == "${aws:InstanceId}"


def test_agent_logfile_lives_in_a_run_as_user_owned_directory():
    """B1: a sink in root-owned /var/log makes the agent exit 1 before doing any work."""
    cfg = _render_agent_config()
    logfile = cfg["agent"]["logfile"]
    assert logfile.startswith(_RUN_AS_USER_OWNED_PREFIXES), (
        f"agent.logfile is {logfile!r}; run_as_user={cfg['agent']['run_as_user']!r} cannot "
        "create or rotate a file in a directory it does not own -- the agent exits 1 before "
        "shipping anything (B1)."
    )


def test_bootstrap_owns_the_agent_log_directory_after_the_user_exists():
    """The `install -d` must come AFTER `dpkg -i` (which creates the cwagent user)."""
    lines = _BOOTSTRAP.read_text().splitlines()
    dpkg_line = next(i for i, l in enumerate(lines, 1) if "dpkg -i /tmp/cw-agent.deb" in l)
    install_line = next(
        (i for i, l in enumerate(lines, 1)
         if "install -d" in l and "amazon-cloudwatch-agent/logs" in l),
        None,
    )
    assert install_line is not None, "no `install -d ... amazon-cloudwatch-agent/logs` in bootstrap"
    assert install_line > dpkg_line, (
        "the agent log directory is chowned to cwagent before the package that creates "
        "that user is installed"
    )


@pytest.mark.parametrize("environment", ["dev", "stage", "prod"])
def test_log_group_and_stream_pairs_are_unique(environment):
    """B3: two tailers on one (group, stream) contend for the sequence token."""
    cfg = _render_agent_config(environment)
    pairs = [
        (e["log_group_name"], e["log_stream_name"])
        for e in cfg["logs"]["logs_collected"]["files"]["collect_list"]
    ]
    dupes = sorted({p for p in pairs if pairs.count(p) > 1})
    assert not dupes, f"duplicate (log_group, log_stream) pairs in the collect_list: {dupes}"


def test_agent_collects_its_own_log():
    """B4: the observability system must observe itself."""
    cfg = _render_agent_config()
    logfile = cfg["agent"]["logfile"]
    paths = [e["file_path"] for e in cfg["logs"]["logs_collected"]["files"]["collect_list"]]
    assert logfile in paths, (
        f"the agent's own log ({logfile}) is not in the collect_list -- its total failure "
        "produces no external signal (B4)."
    )
```

**Exact command:**

```bash
cd backend && python3.11 -m pytest tests/unit/test_bootstrap_cloudwatch_agent.py -v
```

##### I9. Rollback

**Repo half.** One commit touching two files (`infra/scripts/bootstrap-ec2.sh`,
`docs/SIMPLE_AWS_DEPLOYMENT.md`) plus one new test file. `git revert <sha>` is complete and
safe: nothing else in the tree references the new path, and the revert restores a state that is
broken-but-known (today's).

**Host half.** The SSM payload backs up both the source JSON and the translated `.d` copy to
`/root/cwagent-backup-<ts>/` before touching anything. To undo:

```bash
cp -a /root/cwagent-backup-<ts>/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json \
      /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json
/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl \
  -a fetch-config -m ec2 -s -c file:/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json
```

`install -d` leaves an empty owned directory behind. **Do not remove it** - it is inert, and
`/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/logs` is where the vendor default points anyway.

**What is NOT reversible, stated plainly:**

- **There are no EBS snapshots on any root volume, in any environment** [V, dossier Appendix 2].
  `velocityai-dev-root` has zero. There is no filesystem-level rollback for anything this fix
  does on the host. The `/root/cwagent-backup-<ts>/` copies are the only restore point, which is
  why the SSM payload takes them before the first mutation and not after.
- **Log data, once ingested, is billed and cannot be un-ingested.** If the fix causes an
  unexpected ingestion spike (see I6), the mitigation is forward (drop a `collect_list` entry
  and re-run `fetch-config`), not backward.
- **The pre-change backup must capture** exactly two files:
  `/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json` (the source of truth we
  rewrite) and
  `/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.d/file_amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json`
  (what `fetch-config` actually reads). Backing up only the first leaves the agent running the
  old translated config after a partial revert.
- **Blast-radius note:** the SSM command is scoped to one instance id with a `Name` pre-flight.
  There is no path by which it reaches stage or prod. The *repo* change does reach them on their
  next build, and that is not revertable per-environment - see I6's shared-script hazard.

### B2 — `cwagent` cannot read any of the eight configured log files

**Severity:** independently blocking. Fixing B1 alone yields a running agent that ships nothing.
**Confidence:** [V] — permissions and the ACL mask read directly from the instance.

#### Symptom

Even with the agent running, every configured log path would be denied.

#### Root cause

```
$ id cwagent
uid=997(cwagent) gid=986(cwagent) groups=986(cwagent)     <- no supplementary groups

-rw-r----- 1 www-data adm  /var/log/nginx/access.log
-rw-r----- 1 syslog   adm  /var/log/auth.log
-rw-r----- 1 root     adm  /var/log/audit/audit.log

$ sudo -u cwagent test -r /var/log/nginx/access.log ; echo
nginx/access.log: DENIED
```

`cwagent` is in **no supplementary groups**, and every one of those files is group-readable by `adm`
only. `bootstrap-ec2.sh` never runs `usermod -a -G adm cwagent`. [V]

The Docker container logs are the interesting case, and they resolve a puzzle. Bootstrap *does* grant
an ACL for them (`:951-952`, `setfacl -R -m u:cwagent:rX,o::r /var/lib/docker/containers`), which
made a pure-permissions hypothesis look falsified — if the ACL worked, `/velocityai/dev/app` should
have had data. It does not, and here is why:

```
$ getfacl -p /var/lib/docker/containers
user:cwagent:r-x	#effective:--x
group::--x
mask::--x
```

**The mask is `--x`, so the granted read bit is masked off** — effective permission is traverse-only.
Confirmed behaviourally: `sudo -u cwagent ls /var/lib/docker/containers/*/*-json.log` →
`Permission denied`. [V]

#### Why it occurred

The author clearly knew about the permissions problem — the `setfacl` for the Docker path exists
precisely because of it. But it was solved **once, for one path, by the mechanism most likely to be
silently defeated**. `setfacl -m` recalculates the mask from the union of named entries unless `-n`
is passed or the mask is set explicitly; combining `u:cwagent:rX` with `o::r` in a single `-R`
invocation over a tree whose directories have differing base permissions produced a mask that drops
the read bit. Nothing verified the *effective* permission afterwards — only that the command
succeeded.

And the other five paths were never addressed at all, because the failure was invisible: with the
agent crash-looping (B1), no read was ever attempted, so no denial was ever logged.

#### The fix

```bash
usermod -a -G adm cwagent            # covers nginx, auth.log, postgres, audit.log
setfacl -R -m m::rx,u:cwagent:rX /var/lib/docker/containers
setfacl -R -d -m m::rx,u:cwagent:rX /var/lib/docker/containers
systemctl restart amazon-cloudwatch-agent      # required — group membership is read at start
```

Add all of it to `bootstrap-ec2.sh` beside the existing `:951-952`. Note the mask must be set
**explicitly** (`m::rx`) or it will be recalculated and the read bit lost again.

`/var/log/letsencrypt/` is directory-mode `0700 root:root`, so it needs its own ACL if that log is
to be collected; alternatively drop it from the `collect_list`.

#### Verification

For each configured path:
```bash
sudo -u cwagent test -r <path> && echo READABLE || echo DENIED
sudo -u cwagent bash -c 'ls /var/lib/docker/containers/*/*-json.log | head -1'
getfacl -p /var/lib/docker/containers | grep -E 'cwagent|mask'   # effective must include r
```
All eight must be READABLE and the `#effective:` annotation must show `r-x`.

   because it records a reproduced production failure (container DNS). I preserve it; the dossier's
   fix does not.
3. **The project invariants that do bind (INV-3, INV-12, SC-001, Q3) all apply vacuously or
   trivially** - see I7. The only one with real force is **INV-12 / no dual implementation**, which
   is what makes the two duplicated `setfacl` pairs (`:355-356` and `:951-952`) a defect in their
   own right, and what forbids me from adding a third copy.
4. **No characterization golden, no migration, no capability registry entry, and no
   `_KNOWN` counter is in scope.** `find backend/alembic/versions -newer ...` is irrelevant: this fix
   adds no migration (Q3 not triggered - no new table, so no `owner_id`/`workspace_id` obligation).

The single register statement with *indirect* bearing is the dossier's own quotation of
`IMPLEMENTATION-REGISTER.md`'s "goldens 10/10" claim (dossier Appendix 1), which the dossier
already corrects: that figure was measured on `feat/ui-2`, and `dev` is at 10 failed / 6 passed. My
fix touches no Python under `agents/` or `app/`, so it cannot move that number either way - see I8.

##### I3. Root cause - confirmed, corrected, or replaced

The dossier splits B2 into two claims. **The group-membership half is correct and I extend it with
measurements the dossier does not have. The Docker-ACL half is wrong, and because it is wrong the
proposed fix is not durable.**

###### I3.1 The group half - confirmed, and now quantified

`cwagent` has no supplementary groups; the collected files are group-`adm`. That is right. What the
dossier does not establish is *which* of the eight entries `adm` actually solves. I measured all of
them on a stock `ubuntu:24.04` container with the exact package set `bootstrap-ec2.sh:98-104`
installs (`nginx postgresql-16 ... certbot python3-certbot-nginx ufw fail2ban auditd
unattended-upgrades`):

| # | `collect_list` entry (`:988`-`:995`) | Directory | File | `adm` sufficient? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `/var/log/nginx/access.log` | `drwxr-xr-x root:adm` | `-rw-r----- www-data:adm` | **yes** [V] |
| 2 | `/var/log/nginx/error.log` | `drwxr-xr-x root:adm` | `-rw-r----- www-data:adm` | **yes** [V] |
| 3 | `/var/log/postgresql/postgresql-16-main.log` | `drwxrwxr-t root:postgres` (1775, `o=r-x`) | `-rw-r----- postgres:adm` | **yes** [V] |
| 4 | `/var/log/audit/audit.log` | `drwxr-x--- root:adm` (0750) | `0640 root:adm` | **yes** [V on the dir + `auditd.conf`] |
| 5 | `/var/log/auth.log` | `/var/log` is `drwxrwxr-x root:syslog` | `0640 syslog:adm` | **yes** [V on the rsyslog config] |
| 6 | `/var/log/unattended-upgrades/unattended-upgrades.log` | `drwxr-x--- root:adm` (0750) | `-rw-r--r-- root:root` (0644) | **yes** [V] - dir group `adm` gives `r-x`, file is world-readable |
| 7 | `/var/log/letsencrypt/letsencrypt.log` | `drwx------ root:root` (**0700**) | `-rw-r--r-- root:root` (0644) | **NO** - the *directory* blocks it; the file itself is world-readable [V] |
| 8 | `/var/lib/docker/containers/*/*-json.log` | `0710 root:root` parent + `0710 root:root` per container | `0640 root:root` | **NO** - needs an ACL, see I3.2 |

Evidence for the two rows the dossier asserted without checking:

- **Row 4 rebuts the brief's own hypothesis.** The brief warned "`/var/log/audit` is often
  `0700 root:root` regardless of group". On Ubuntu 24.04 it is **`drwxr-x--- root:adm`**, because
  Debian/Ubuntu ship `log_group = adm` in `/etc/audit/auditd.conf` (verified: the shipped conf's
  non-comment body contains `log_group = adm`). auditd chowns `audit.log` to `root:<log_group>` and
  chmods it 0640. So `adm` **is** the right group for audit, and the dossier's
  `-rw-r----- 1 root adm /var/log/audit/audit.log` observation is consistent with the distro
  default rather than a local customisation. `auditd` *is* installed by
  `bootstrap-ec2.sh:102` (`ufw fail2ban auditd`).
- **Row 3.** `pg_createcluster` creates the log file explicitly: `chmod 0640, $real_logfile` at
  `/usr/bin/pg_createcluster:434`, then `$g = (getgrnam 'adm')[2]` at `:437` and
  `lchown $owneruid, $g, $real_logfile` at `:441`. Measured result: `-rw-r----- postgres adm
  postgresql-16-main.log`. The *directory* is 1775 `root:postgres`, i.e. world-traversable, so only
  the file's group matters.
- **Row 5.** `/etc/rsyslog.conf:37-39` ships `$FileOwner syslog`, `$FileGroup adm`,
  `$FileCreateMode 0640`.
- **Row 7.** certbot 2.9.0 created `/var/log/letsencrypt` as `drwx------ root root` and
  `letsencrypt.log` as `-rw-r--r-- root root`. **The file is already world-readable; only the
  0700 directory is in the way.** That materially changes the fix (I5 step 3).

**Net: `usermod -a -G adm cwagent` alone fixes six of the eight entries.** The dossier's one-line
comment "covers nginx, auth.log, postgres, audit.log" undercounts (it omits unattended-upgrades)
and overstates for letsencrypt.

**Ordering is real, and I proved it.** Supplementary groups are captured at process start
(`setgroups`/`initgroups`), never re-read. Measured:

```
-- read as cwagent WITH adm supplementary group:
    READ: OK
-- read as cwagent WITHOUT supplementary groups (process started before usermod):
    READ: DENIED
```

So the `usermod` must precede the process start, and the already-running agent must be restarted.
In `bootstrap-ec2.sh` the start happens at `:1005-1007` (`fetch-config -s`, whose wrapper ends in
`systemctl restart`), so the `usermod` must sit between `:947` (after `dpkg -i` creates the user)
and `:1005`. Placing it immediately after the `dpkg` block is correct.

###### I3.2 The Docker half - the dossier's root cause is wrong; here is the real one

The dossier says:

> `setfacl -m` recalculates the mask from the union of named entries unless `-n` is passed or the
> mask is set explicitly; combining `u:cwagent:rX` with `o::r` in a single `-R` invocation over a
> tree whose directories have differing base permissions produced a mask that drops the read bit.

I reproduced the exact command on a fresh 0710 directory in `ubuntu:24.04`. **setfacl's own output
is correct** - the mask is recalculated to the *union*, which includes read:

```
===== E1  setfacl -m u:cwagent:rX,o::r on a fresh 0710 dir  (mask recalculated?) =====
before mode=710 owner=root:root
after  mode=754
    # file: /t1
    user::rwx
    user:cwagent:r-x
    group::--x
    mask::r-x            <-- read bit PRESENT
    other::r--
```

So the command as written does the right thing. The dossier's mechanism is not what happened.
The next experiment shows what did:

```
===== E2  now chmod 0710 /t1 =====
after chmod mode=710
    user::rwx
    user:cwagent:r-x	#effective:--x
    group::--x
    mask::--x            <-- read bit GONE
    other::---
-- can cwagent list the dir?
    LIST: DENIED
```

That is **byte-for-byte the state the dossier measured on the live box** - including the loss of
`o::r`, which the dossier's excerpt did not quote but which is implied by the same `chmod`.

The reason is the POSIX-ACL/`chmod` interaction: on an inode carrying an extended ACL, the *group*
bits of `st_mode` are the **mask**, not `group::`. A `chmod 0710` therefore rewrites the mask to
`--x` and zeroes `other::`, leaving `group::` untouched - exactly the observed shape.

**Who runs that `chmod`?** `dockerd`. Reproduced end to end with a nested daemon
(`docker.io` 29.1.3 on Ubuntu 24.04, one version family off the box's Docker CE):

```
===== apply bootstrap-ec2.sh :951-952 verbatim =====
after setfacl: mode=754
  user:cwagent:r-x
  mask::r-x
  other::r--
  default:mask::r-x
  default:other::r--

===== kill dockerd, restart it  <-- discriminating step =====
while stopped: mode=754

===== RESULT after dockerd restart =====
mode=710 owner=root:root
  user:cwagent:r-x	#effective:--x
  mask::--x
  other::---
  default:mask::r-x          <-- default ACL SURVIVES
  default:other::r--
```

`dockerd` calls `MkdirAllAndChown(<data-root>/containers, 0710, ...)` at startup, whose
`setPermissions` helper chmods whenever `stat.Mode().Perm() != mode.Perm()`. Since **any** ACL that
gives `cwagent` an effective read bit necessarily raises the mode above 0710 (mask `r-x` -> group
bits `5`), `stat != 0710` is guaranteed and the chmod is guaranteed. This is a **structural
conflict, not a race**: a one-shot `setfacl` cannot survive a daemon restart, no matter how it is
written.

**A second, independent mechanism breaks it even without a restart.** New per-container directories
are created mode 0710. POSIX default-ACL inheritance intersects the inherited mask with the
creation mode's group bits:

```
===== E4  DEFAULT ACL inheritance -> new SUBDIR created mode 0710 =====
-- parent:
    mask::r-x
    default:mask::r-x
-- new subdir (mkdir 0710):
    user:cwagent:r-x	#effective:--x
    mask::--x            <-- born masked
    default:mask::r-x
-- can cwagent list the new subdir?
    LIST: DENIED

===== E5  new FILE created mode 0640 =====
    user:cwagent:r-x	#effective:r--
    mask::r--
-- can cwagent read the json log?
    READ: OK
-- can cwagent GLOB /t4/*/*-json.log ?
    ls: cannot access '/t4/*/*-json.log': No such file or directory
```

This is the answer to the brief's question *"do new container dirs inherit the default ACL? this is
why `-d` matters; prove it"*. They inherit the **entries** but are born with mask `--x`, so `-d` is
necessary but **not sufficient**. The json log *file* is readable (E5), but the agent can never
reach it because it cannot enumerate either directory level.

`docker compose up -d --remove-orphans` runs on **every** CI deploy (`infra/buildspec.yml:298`), and
recreating a container creates a new `<id>` directory. So mechanism 2 fires on every deploy, and
mechanism 1 on every reboot or `systemctl restart docker`.

**Causal chain, trigger to symptom:**

1. Bootstrap runs `setfacl` once at `:951-952`. Correct at that instant (mask `r-x`, mode 0754).
2. Section 17 starts the containers. Each `<id>` dir is created 0710 -> inherited mask `--x`
   (E4). The glob is already dead **on a pristine first boot, before any reboot**.
3. The first `systemctl restart docker` / reboot / Docker-CE upgrade chmods the parent back to 0710
   -> parent mask `--x` (E2, dind) -> even the top-level enumeration dies, and `o::r` is lost.
4. `sudo -u cwagent ls /var/lib/docker/containers/*/*-json.log` -> `Permission denied`, exactly as
   the dossier observed.
5. `/velocityai/dev/app` is empty. Because B1 keeps the agent crash-looping, no denial was ever
   even attempted, so nothing surfaced.

**The root cause, at the level of a broken assumption:** the design assumed a filesystem permission
grant is a one-time provisioning act. For `/var/lib/docker/containers` that assumption is false -
the directory is *owned by a reconciling daemon* that re-asserts mode 0710 as an invariant, and the
kernel's default-ACL inheritance re-applies that invariant to every child. Any grant here must be a
**reconciler**, not a one-shot. That is why the fix changes shape, not just arguments.

###### I3.3 Why the dossier's proposed fix does not hold

```bash
setfacl -R -m m::rx,u:cwagent:rX /var/lib/docker/containers
setfacl -R -d -m m::rx,u:cwagent:rX /var/lib/docker/containers
```

- Setting `m::rx` explicitly *is* correct as far as it goes - it produces mask `r-x` (E3, first
  half). But mode then becomes 0750, and the very next `dockerd` start chmods to 0710 and the mask
  is `--x` again (E3, second half). Verified.
- It does nothing for mechanism 2: the next `docker compose up -d` mints an `<id>` dir with mask
  `--x` regardless.
- It **drops `o::r`**. `setfacl -m` only modifies the entries named, so today's `other::` is left
  as-is - which after `dockerd`'s chmod is `---`. The default ACL keeps `default:other::r--`
  (chmod does not touch default ACLs, E6), so the container-DNS incident does not immediately
  recur; but the fix as written silently abandons a documented, load-bearing grant.
- The dossier's alternative "`-n` is passed" is **actively harmful**: `-n` suppresses mask
  recalculation, so the inherited `--x` mask stays and the read bit is masked off from the start.
  Measured:

  ```
  ===== E3b  setfacl -n -m u:cwagent:rX (no mask recalculation) =====
      user:cwagent:r-x	#effective:--x
      mask::--x
  ```

##### I4. Blast-radius sweep - every place this reaches

###### I4.1 Enumerate every path in the agent's `collect_list`

Counted from the file, not from the dossier. `bootstrap-ec2.sh:987` opens `collect_list`; the
entries are one per line, `:988`-`:995`. **Eight entries.** For each: the owner/group/mode it will
have on the box, and which mechanism grants `cwagent` read after the fix.

| # | Path | Log group | Owner:group / mode on the box | Grant mechanism after the fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `/var/log/nginx/access.log` | `nginx-access` | `www-data:adm 0640`, dir `root:adm 0755` | **group `adm`** |
| 2 | `/var/log/nginx/error.log` | `nginx-error` | `www-data:adm 0640`, dir `root:adm 0755` | **group `adm`** |
| 3 | `/var/log/postgresql/postgresql-16-main.log` | `postgres` | `postgres:adm 0640`, dir `root:postgres 1775` | **group `adm`** (dir is `o=r-x`) |
| 4 | `/var/log/audit/audit.log` | `system` | `root:adm 0640`, dir `root:adm 0750` | **group `adm`** |
| 5 | `/var/log/auth.log` | `auth` | `syslog:adm 0640`, dir `/var/log` `root:syslog 0775` | **group `adm`** |
| 6 | `/var/log/unattended-upgrades/unattended-upgrades.log` | `system` | `root:root 0644`, dir `root:adm 0750` | **group `adm`** on the dir; the file is world-readable |
| 7 | `/var/log/letsencrypt/letsencrypt.log` | `letsencrypt` | `root:root 0644`, dir `root:root **0700**` | **directory mode change** (`chgrp adm` + `chmod 0750`); the file needs nothing |
| 8 | `/var/lib/docker/containers/*/*-json.log` (**glob**, N=2 today) | `app` | files `root:root 0640`; parent dir and each `<id>` dir `root:root 0710` | **ACL, re-asserted by a systemd reconciler** |

After **B4** lands there will be a ninth entry, `/var/log/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.log`. **B1's fix
already makes it readable** (`install -o cwagent -g cwagent -m 0644`) - the agent owns its own log.
No group or ACL work is needed for it, and the agent's internal rotation writes the rotated files
as the same uid. I state this so B4's executor does not add redundant permission work.

###### I4.2 logrotate - the ripple the dossier does not cover

**No logrotate configuration is authored by this repository.** Verified:

```
$ grep -rn 'logrotate' infra/ docker-compose.yml
(no output)
```

Every rotation is distro-package-owned. I read each shipped config in a container with the exact
bootstrap package set and simulated the rotation.

| Path | Governing config | Directives that matter | Does the grant survive? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/var/log/nginx/*.log` | `/etc/logrotate.d/nginx` | `daily`, `rotate 14`, `compress delaycompress`, **`create 0640 www-data adm`**, `sharedscripts`, `postrotate invoke-rc.d nginx rotate` | **YES.** `create` names group `adm` explicitly. Simulated: recreated `access.log` is `-rw-r----- 1 www-data adm`. [V] |
| `/var/log/auth.log` | `/etc/logrotate.d/rsyslog` | `weekly`, `rotate 4`, no `create`, `postrotate /usr/lib/rsyslog/rsyslog-rotate` | **YES.** No `create` means logrotate renames and rsyslog recreates on HUP, using `$FileOwner syslog` / `$FileGroup adm` / `$FileCreateMode 0640` from `/etc/rsyslog.conf:37-39`. |
| `/var/log/postgresql/*.log` | `/etc/logrotate.d/postgresql-common` | `weekly`, `rotate 10`, **`copytruncate`**, `su root root` | **YES, trivially.** `copytruncate` preserves the inode, so ownership *and* any ACL survive untouched. Proven: E8b showed an ACL intact across a `copytruncate` rotation. |
| `/var/log/audit/audit.log` | **none** - no `/etc/logrotate.d/audit*` exists | auditd self-rotates: `max_log_file = 8` (MB), `num_logs = 5`, `max_log_file_action = ROTATE`, `log_group = adm` | **YES.** auditd applies `log_group` to the file it creates. |
| `/var/log/unattended-upgrades/*.log` | `/etc/logrotate.d/unattended-upgrades` | `monthly`, `rotate 6`, no `create`, no `su` | **YES.** No `create` -> logrotate does not recreate; `unattended-upgrade` recreates it via `logging.basicConfig` under umask 022 -> `0644 root:root`, inside a `0750 root:adm` dir. |
| `/var/log/letsencrypt/*.log` | `/etc/logrotate.d/certbot` | `weekly`, `rotate 12`, `compress`, `missingok`, no `create`, no `su` | **YES, given the fix.** The grant is on the **directory**, and neither logrotate nor certbot chmods an existing log directory (certbot's `make_or_verify_dir` runs with `strict_permissions` off by default and only sets the mode at creation). The recreated file is `0644 root:root`, readable through the now-`adm` directory. |
| `/var/lib/docker/containers/*/*-json.log` | **none** - no logrotate involvement | Docker's own json-file rotation: `docker-compose.yml:130-138` and `:181-185` set `max-size: "100m"`, `max-file: "5"` for **both** services | **YES for the file, given the fix.** A rotated `<id>-json.log` is created inside the `<id>` dir, so it inherits the default ACL, and its mask is `default_mask AND 0640's group bits` = `r--` -> `u:cwagent` effective `r--` (E5). Enumeration still depends on the reconciler, which is exactly what the reconciler is for. |

**And the question the brief asked directly - does a default ACL survive rotation and new-file
creation?** Measured both ways:

```
===== E8  logrotate 'create 0640 www-data adm' with a default ACL on the dir =====
-- ACL of the RECREATED /t8/access.log:
    user:cwagent:r--
    group::r-x	#effective:r--
    mask::r--
```

The recreated file **does** inherit the parent's default ACL, and the mask is intersected with the
`create` mode's group bits. So a default ACL is a durable grant across `create`-style rotation.

```
===== E8b  copytruncate =====
-- ACL after copytruncate rotation (same inode -> ACL kept?):
    user:cwagent:r--
    mask::r--
```

Unchanged, as expected for an inode-preserving truncate.

**What the fix must add for durability, stated as the brief demands:** for the six `adm` paths,
nothing - group membership is an attribute of the *reading process*, entirely orthogonal to
rotation, and every rotation path re-creates the file with group `adm` or leaves it world-readable
inside an `adm` directory. For letsencrypt, the grant must be on the **directory**, not the file,
precisely so that certbot's recreation of `letsencrypt.log` cannot revoke it. For Docker, no
static grant is durable at all, which is why the fix installs a reconciler.

###### I4.3 The Docker ACL mask mechanics (the brief's second question, answered with measurements)

- **Does `setfacl -m` recalculate the mask?** Yes, to the union of `group::` and all named entries.
  Measured (E1): `u:cwagent:rX` on a 0710 dir -> `mask::r-x`. The dossier's claim that the
  recalculation *dropped* the read bit is false.
- **Is `-n` required?** No - and it is counterproductive. With `-n` the pre-existing `--x` mask is
  left in place and the named entry is masked off (E3b). The dossier lists `-n` as one of the two
  ways to avoid the (non-existent) problem; following that advice would leave the bug in place.
- **Is an explicit `m::` required?** Yes, but for a different reason than the dossier gives. On the
  *parent* the union recalculation already yields `r-x`, so `m::` is redundant there. On a
  **freshly created `<id>` subdirectory** the inherited mask is `--x` and `group::` is `--x`, so
  the union is still `--x` - the recalculation cannot rescue it. Only an explicit mask does. That
  is the real justification for `m::rX`.
- **Recursive plus default.** Both are needed and they do different jobs: `-R -m` fixes the
  directories that exist *now* (including every `<id>` dir born masked), `-R -d -m` seeds the
  default ACL so *files* created later (rotated json logs, per-container `/etc/hosts`) inherit the
  named entry. Neither substitutes for the other, and neither is durable against `dockerd`'s chmod
  or a new `mkdir 0710` - hence the reconciler.
- **Containers created after the ACL is applied.** Proven in E4: they inherit the entries with mask
  `--x` and are not listable. This is the single most important correction in this report, because
  it means the failure recurs on **every deploy**, not only on reboot.

###### I4.4 Security consequence of `adm`, and whether `adm` is the right group everywhere

`adm` on Debian/Ubuntu is the conventional "read system logs" group. Adding `cwagent` to it grants
read on: nginx access+error, `auth.log` (which contains sudo/sshd records), `syslog`, `kern.log`,
`mail.log`, `audit.log`, the postgres cluster log, and the unattended-upgrades logs.

**Worth stating, and my assessment:** this is a *widening* of what the log-shipping daemon can read
beyond the eight configured paths - it can read every `adm` log on the box, not only the ones in
`collect_list`. Three things bound the risk to acceptable:

1. It is **read-only** and confers no write, no execute, and no group ownership of anything.
2. The agent already has an IAM role that can `PutLogEvents` to `/velocityai/dev/*`; the *content*
   of `auth.log` and `audit.log` is already destined for CloudWatch by design
   (`monitoring/main.tf:12-13` names `auth` as a log group and the module's variable docstring at
   `variables.tf:28` explicitly reasons about "auth/auditd long-forensics" retention). Group `adm`
   is the mechanism the distro provides for exactly this.
3. It is **narrower than the alternatives.** `run_as_user: root` (I11) grants everything; the
   `docker` group is root-equivalent (the `bootstrap-ec2.sh:340` comment already says so).

`adm` is the right group for entries 1-6 - verified per-path in I3.1, including the two the brief
flagged: `audit.log` (Ubuntu ships `log_group = adm`, dir `0750 root:adm`) and postgres
(`pg_createcluster` chowns to `postgres:adm`). It is **not** the right mechanism for entry 7
(letsencrypt: the directory is `root:root`, so a group grant needs a `chgrp` anyway - at which
point `chgrp adm` + `chmod 0750` *is* the group mechanism, consistently with the other five log
directories) and it is **not available** for entry 8 (Docker's dirs are `root:root` and dockerd
chowns them back).

##### I5. The complete fix

Two halves. The **repo half** (`infra/scripts/bootstrap-ec2.sh`) is durable - it survives an
instance rebuild and is re-uploaded to
`s3://velocityai-dev-pg-dumps-577954642302/config/bootstrap-ec2.sh` by the existing
`$TF/app apply` on any `dev` push (`infra/terraform/app/main.tf:79-94`). The **host half** (an SSM
`send-command`) is what actually changes the running box today, and it **evaporates** if the
instance is ever replaced (root volume `delete_on_termination = true`, zero snapshots). Both are
required; they are complements, not alternatives.

###### Step 1 - delete the duplicate section-8 `setfacl` pair (INV-12)

**File:** `infra/scripts/bootstrap-ec2.sh` -- **anchor:** the comment block ending at `:354` and the
two commands at `:355-356`.

BEFORE (`:339-356`):

```bash
# POSIX ACL so cwagent can read /var/lib/docker/containers/*.log without
# being in the docker group (docker.sock = root-equivalent). `|| true`
# because the cwagent user may not exist yet — repeated after cwagent install
# in §13.
#
# `o::r` is intentional and load-bearing. /var/lib/docker/containers is
# mode 0710 by default — owner:root, group:root, other:---. When setfacl
# sets a default ACL it inherits the dir's current "other" bits as the
# default for new files. That meant new container bind-mount files
# (notably /etc/hosts, which docker generates per container and bind-mounts
# in) got mode 0640 — readable only by root and the cwagent named entry.
# Containers running as a non-root user (our Dockerfile sets uid 10001
# `velocityai`) then can't read /etc/hosts and DNS lookups for entries we
# added via `extra_hosts: host.docker.internal:host-gateway` fail with
# "Temporary failure in name resolution". Forcing `o::r` here restores the
# normal world-readable /etc/hosts so app containers can use the host.
setfacl -R -m u:cwagent:rX,o::r /var/lib/docker/containers || true
setfacl -R -d -m u:cwagent:rX,o::r /var/lib/docker/containers || true
```

AFTER:

```bash
# The POSIX ACL that lets `cwagent` read /var/lib/docker/containers/*/*-json.log
# is NOT granted here. It cannot be granted once: `dockerd` chmods this
# directory back to 0710 at every daemon start (which rewrites the ACL mask and
# zeroes the read bit), and every new per-container directory is created 0710
# so it inherits the default ACL with the mask already masked off. The grant is
# therefore a reconciler — /usr/local/sbin/velocityai-cwagent-docker-acl, driven
# by a systemd timer — installed in §14 once the `cwagent` user exists. See the
# header of that script for the full mechanism and the load-bearing `o::r`.
```

*Why this and not leaving the pair in place with `|| true`:* it is a second copy of the same grant
that provably does not hold (INV-12), and at this point in the script the `cwagent` user does not
exist, so `setfacl` fails outright and `|| true` swallows it. It has never done anything. The stale
"section 13" reference in the old comment is also wrong (the twin is in section 14).

###### Step 2 - add the group grant, correctly ordered

**File:** `infra/scripts/bootstrap-ec2.sh` -- **anchor:** immediately after the `fi` closing the
`dpkg -i` block (currently `:947`), and before the reconciler install.

BEFORE (`:941-952`):

```bash
# ── 14. CloudWatch agent ───────────────────────────────────────────────
if ! dpkg -s amazon-cloudwatch-agent >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    wget -q https://s3.amazonaws.com/amazoncloudwatch-agent/ubuntu/amd64/latest/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.deb \
        -O /tmp/cw-agent.deb
    dpkg -i /tmp/cw-agent.deb
    rm /tmp/cw-agent.deb
fi
# Re-grant ACL now that cwagent user exists. See §8 above for why o::r is
# load-bearing (preserves world-read on per-container /etc/hosts so non-
# root containers can do DNS).
setfacl -R -m u:cwagent:rX,o::r /var/lib/docker/containers
setfacl -R -d -m u:cwagent:rX,o::r /var/lib/docker/containers
```

AFTER:

```bash
# ── 14. CloudWatch agent ───────────────────────────────────────────────
if ! dpkg -s amazon-cloudwatch-agent >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    wget -q https://s3.amazonaws.com/amazoncloudwatch-agent/ubuntu/amd64/latest/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.deb \
        -O /tmp/cw-agent.deb
    dpkg -i /tmp/cw-agent.deb
    rm /tmp/cw-agent.deb
fi

# The agent runs as `cwagent` (see "run_as_user" below). Six of the eight
# collect_list paths are readable through the distro's conventional log-reader
# group on Ubuntu 24.04 — nginx access/error (0640 www-data:adm), postgres
# (0640 postgres:adm via pg_createcluster), audit.log (0640 root:adm; auditd.conf
# ships log_group = adm), auth.log (0640 syslog:adm via rsyslog's $FileGroup),
# and unattended-upgrades (0644 root:root inside a 0750 root:adm directory).
#
# Supplementary groups are read once, at process start. This MUST run before the
# `fetch-config -s` below, whose ctl wrapper restarts the agent; a usermod after
# the agent is already running has no effect until the next restart.
usermod -a -G adm cwagent

# /var/log/letsencrypt is 0700 root:root (certbot's own default) while
# letsencrypt.log inside it is already 0644 — so the DIRECTORY is the only thing
# in the way. Bring it to the same convention as the other log directories.
# Durable: certbot does not re-chmod an existing log dir (make_or_verify_dir runs
# with strict_permissions off by default), and /etc/logrotate.d/certbot declares
# no `create`/`su`, so rotation cannot revoke it either.
mkdir -p /var/log/letsencrypt
chgrp adm /var/log/letsencrypt
chmod 0750 /var/log/letsencrypt

# The Docker container-log ACL is a RECONCILER, not a one-shot — see the script
# header for why. Install it, arm the timer, and run it once now.
install -m 0755 /dev/null /usr/local/sbin/velocityai-cwagent-docker-acl
cat > /usr/local/sbin/velocityai-cwagent-docker-acl <<'ACLSCRIPT'
#!/bin/bash
# Re-assert the POSIX ACL that lets the CloudWatch agent's `cwagent` user read
# the Docker json-file container logs.
#
# WHY THIS IS A RECONCILER AND NOT A ONE-SHOT
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# /var/lib/docker/containers is mode 0710 root:root. On an inode carrying an
# extended ACL the GROUP bits of st_mode are the ACL MASK, so any grant that
# gives cwagent an effective read bit necessarily raises the mode above 0710.
# Two independent mechanisms then revert it:
#
#   1. dockerd calls MkdirAllAndChown(<data-root>/containers, 0710, ...) at every
#      daemon start, whose setPermissions helper chmods whenever the current mode
#      differs from 0710. chmod on an ACL-bearing inode rewrites the MASK, so the
#      read bit is zeroed. Because a working grant ALWAYS leaves mode != 0710,
#      this chmod is guaranteed, not racy. Fires on `systemctl restart docker`,
#      on reboot, and on a docker-ce package upgrade.
#
#   2. Each per-container <id> directory is created mode 0710. POSIX default-ACL
#      inheritance intersects the inherited mask with the creation mode's group
#      bits, so a NEW container directory is born with mask --x however correct
#      the parent's default ACL is. Fires on every `docker compose up -d` that
#      recreates a container, i.e. on every deploy.
#
# A single setfacl at provisioning time therefore cannot hold. The systemd timer
# beside this script re-runs it; the agent re-evaluates its glob and picks the
# files up.
#
# WHY `m::rX` IS EXPLICIT
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# `setfacl -m` recalculates the mask as the UNION of group:: and the named
# entries. On the parent that already yields r-x. But on a freshly created <id>
# directory both group:: and the inherited mask are --x, so the union is still
# --x and the recalculation cannot rescue it. Only an explicit mask does. (Do NOT
# use `-n`: it suppresses recalculation entirely and leaves the read bit masked.)
#
# WHY `o::r` STAYS
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# /var/lib/docker/containers defaults to other::---, and the DEFAULT ACL is what
# per-container bind-mount files inherit — notably the /etc/hosts docker
# generates per container. Without world-read there, a container running as the
# non-root uid 10001 our Dockerfile sets cannot read /etc/hosts, and every DNS
# lookup for the `extra_hosts: host.docker.internal:host-gateway` entry fails
# with "Temporary failure in name resolution". This was a real production
# failure; do not drop it.
set -u
DIR=/var/lib/docker/containers
[ -d "$DIR" ] || exit 0
id -u cwagent >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0
setfacl -R -m  m::rX,u:cwagent:rX,o::r "$DIR" || exit 1
setfacl -R -d -m m::rX,u:cwagent:rX,o::r "$DIR" || exit 1
exit 0
ACLSCRIPT
chmod 0755 /usr/local/sbin/velocityai-cwagent-docker-acl

cat > /etc/systemd/system/velocityai-cwagent-docker-acl.service <<'ACLUNIT'
[Unit]
Description=Re-assert the cwagent read ACL on Docker container logs
Documentation=file:/usr/local/sbin/velocityai-cwagent-docker-acl
After=docker.service

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/sbin/velocityai-cwagent-docker-acl
ACLUNIT

cat > /etc/systemd/system/velocityai-cwagent-docker-acl.timer <<'ACLTIMER'
[Unit]
Description=Periodically re-assert the cwagent read ACL on Docker container logs

[Timer]
OnBootSec=2min
OnUnitActiveSec=1min
AccuracySec=10s
Unit=velocityai-cwagent-docker-acl.service

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
ACLTIMER

systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl enable --now velocityai-cwagent-docker-acl.timer
systemctl start velocityai-cwagent-docker-acl.service
```

Note the `install -m 0755 /dev/null <path>` before the heredoc: it creates the file with the right
mode atomically even on a re-run where the previous file was left non-executable. The trailing
`chmod 0755` is belt-and-braces for the case where the file already existed.

*Why a timer and not a `.path` unit:* a `systemd.path` unit with `PathModified=` would fire the
instant a container directory appears, which is more elegant. I cannot verify systemd's inotify
mask for `PathModified=` on a **directory** offline, and an unverified trigger that silently never
fires is exactly the failure class this whole dossier is about. The timer's semantics are
unambiguous and its worst case is a bounded delay (see I6). The `.path` unit is recorded as a
deferred optimisation in I12.

*Why `OnUnitActiveSec=1min` and not something longer:* the work is two `setfacl` calls over a tree
of two container directories - microseconds. The cost of a shorter period is nil; the cost of a
longer one is a longer gap in the `/app` log group after a deploy.

###### Step 3 - nothing changes in the `collect_list`

`/var/log/letsencrypt/letsencrypt.log` **stays** at `:994`. Removing it would leave
`aws_cloudwatch_log_metric_filter.cert_renew_failure` (`monitoring/main.tf:758`) and
`aws_cloudwatch_log_metric_filter.cert_renew_success` (`:805`) attached to a log group nothing
writes, and the success-side heartbeat alarm is `treat_missing_data = "breaching"` - so dropping
the path would *create* a new permanent false alarm, adding to the 41 already firing in B6. The
directory fix in step 2 is three commands and durable; dropping is not free. This is the answer to
the brief's "collect-with-ACL vs drop-from-collect_list" question: **collect, and fix the
directory mode rather than adding an ACL** (an ACL is unnecessary here - the file is already
world-readable, only the directory blocks the path).

B3 (stream-name collisions) and B4 (add the agent's own log) also edit this list. My change does
not touch it, so the three are textually disjoint. See I10.

###### Step 4 - the host half (applies to the running box; evaporates on instance replacement)

Per C1's rules: **never `--targets`** (six tag values are byte-identical across dev/stage/prod);
always `--instance-ids`, with a `Name` guard.

```bash
DEV=i-092d5961f5aca87a6
NAME=$(aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids "$DEV" \
  --query 'Reservations[0].Instances[0].Tags[?Key==`Name`].Value|[0]' --output text)
[ "$NAME" = "velocityai-dev-app" ] || { echo "REFUSING: $DEV is '$NAME'"; exit 1; }

cat > /tmp/b2-payload.sh <<'PAYLOAD'
set -euo pipefail
TS=$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)
BK=/root/cwagent-acl-backup-$TS
mkdir -p "$BK"

# Capture the pre-change state so I9's rollback has something to restore.
id cwagent                                   > "$BK/id-cwagent.before"  2>&1 || true
getfacl -p /var/lib/docker/containers        > "$BK/containers.acl.before" 2>&1 || true
stat -c '%a %U:%G' /var/log/letsencrypt      > "$BK/letsencrypt.mode.before" 2>&1 || true
ls -l /etc/systemd/system/velocityai-cwagent-docker-acl.* \
                                             > "$BK/units.before" 2>&1 || true

# 1) group membership (idempotent: usermod -aG on an existing member is a no-op)
usermod -a -G adm cwagent

# 2) letsencrypt directory
mkdir -p /var/log/letsencrypt
chgrp adm /var/log/letsencrypt
chmod 0750 /var/log/letsencrypt

# 3) the reconciler + timer  (identical bytes to the bootstrap section-14 block)
# <<< paste the /usr/local/sbin/velocityai-cwagent-docker-acl heredoc,
#     the .service heredoc, and the .timer heredoc from Step 2 verbatim here >>>
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl enable --now velocityai-cwagent-docker-acl.timer
systemctl start velocityai-cwagent-docker-acl.service

# 4) restart the agent so it re-execs and picks up the adm supplementary group.
#    (B1 must already have created /var/log/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.log, or the
#     agent will still crash-loop on its own sink — see I10.)
systemctl restart amazon-cloudwatch-agent

echo "BACKUP=$BK"
PAYLOAD

jq -Rs '{commands: [.]}' /tmp/b2-payload.sh > /tmp/b2-params.json
aws ssm send-command --instance-ids "$DEV" \
  --document-name AWS-RunShellScript \
  --comment "B2: cwagent log readability" \
  --timeout-seconds 600 \
  --parameters file:///tmp/b2-params.json \
  --region eu-central-1
```

Every step is idempotent: `usermod -aG` on an existing member is a no-op, `mkdir -p`/`chgrp`/`chmod`
converge, the heredocs overwrite byte-identically, and `systemctl enable --now` on an already-armed
timer is a no-op.

###### Step 5 - what is deleted (INV-12)

- `infra/scripts/bootstrap-ec2.sh:355-356` - the section-8 `setfacl` pair (never worked; the user
  does not exist yet at that point).
- `infra/scripts/bootstrap-ec2.sh:951-952` - the section-14 `setfacl` pair, **superseded** by the
  reconciler script. Not left beside it.

After the change there is exactly **one** implementation of the Docker ACL grant
(`/usr/local/sbin/velocityai-cwagent-docker-acl`) with two invocations of it (once at provisioning,
then by the timer). Two *triggers* of one implementation is not a dual implementation; two copies
of the `setfacl` commands would be, which is what exists today.

None. No settings key, no environment variable, no Terraform variable. The timer period is a
literal in the unit file with its reasoning in the comment above it; making it a variable would add

##### I6. Ripple-effect analysis - why nothing else breaks

Assume the fix is wrong. Where does it bite?

**1. `usermod -a -G adm cwagent` aborts bootstrap if group `adm` is missing.** `set -euo pipefail`
is in force (`:26`), so a failure aborts before sections 16/17 (the pg_dump cron and the app
service). `adm` is created by `base-passwd`, is present on every Ubuntu image, and is already
depended on implicitly by `rsyslog`/`auditd`/`nginx` packaging. If it were somehow absent, failing
loudly at provisioning is the correct outcome and matches B5's philosophy. **Verified present** in
the probe container: `adm:x:4:ubuntu`.

**2. Does the agent actually honour supplementary groups?** **This is the one load-bearing thing I
could not verify, and I am flagging it rather than asserting it.** The shipped systemd unit
(`/etc/systemd/system/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.service`, read from the current
`amazon-cloudwatch-agent.deb`) has **no `User=`**:

```
[Service]
Type=simple
ExecStart=/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/start-amazon-cloudwatch-agent
KillMode=process
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=60s
```

and `amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl` (459 lines) contains no `runas`/`run_as_user` handling. So the
agent starts as root and drops privileges **itself**, inside the Go binary, from the config's
`run_as_user`. Whether that drop uses `setgroups(execUser.Sgids)` (which honours `/etc/group`) or a
bare `setuid` (which would not) I could not confirm: I ran the real binary under Rosetta and it
exited before `/proc/<pid>/status` could be sampled, and `strings` over the stripped binary
returned nothing for the symbol names. **[I]** - my belief, from the agent's use of the
`libcontainer/user` resolver, is that supplementary groups *are* applied, and AWS's guidance to
grant the `cwagent` user read access to log files only makes sense on that assumption. **The fix
carries its own proof:** I8 test T3 is an on-box `grep Groups /proc/<agent-pid>/status` that must
show `4` (adm). If it does not, the fix as specified is insufficient for entries 1-6 and the
decision escalates to I11's `run_as_user: root` option. The executor must run T3 before declaring
B2 done.

**3. The letsencrypt directory mode change breaks certbot.** Considered and rejected. certbot's
`util.set_up_core_dir` -> `make_or_verify_dir(directory, mode, uid, strict)` runs with
`strict=config.strict_permissions`, which is **False** by default; with `strict` false it verifies
ownership only, not mode, and does not chmod an existing directory. Ownership is unchanged (`root`
stays the owner; only the group changes). `certbot.timer` renewals therefore continue unaffected.
Residual: if an operator ever passes `--strict-permissions`, certbot would complain. That flag is
not used anywhere in the repo (`grep -rn 'strict-permissions' infra/` -> no output).

**4. Widening `/var/log/letsencrypt` from 0700 to 0750 root:adm exposes ACME material.** The
directory holds `letsencrypt.log*` only; private keys live under `/etc/letsencrypt/`, which is not
touched. The log does contain hostnames and ACME account URLs, which are already going to
CloudWatch by design (that is the whole point of collecting it).

**5. The reconciler's `o::r` makes json container logs world-readable.** True - and it is the
**status quo**, not a new exposure: `bootstrap-ec2.sh:951` already applies `-R ... o::r` to the
whole tree today. I deliberately did not tighten it in the same change (one variable at a time),
because `o::r` is what the section-8 comment records as load-bearing for container DNS. Tightening
it to the default ACL only is recorded in I12 as a separate, testable follow-up.

**6. The timer runs `setfacl -R` forever on a growing tree.** `/var/lib/docker/containers` holds one
directory per *existing* container - two today (`backend`, `frontend`), transiently three during a
compose recreate. Stopped-and-removed containers have their directories deleted by Docker. The tree
does not grow. Worst case is a handful of inodes per minute.

**7. Timer versus a new container: how long is the gap?** Up to 60 s from the `mkdir` to the ACL
re-assert. During that window the agent's glob cannot see the new file. The agent re-evaluates
`file_path` globs on its own schedule, so the file is picked up on the next scan after the ACL
lands. **[I]** on the agent's exact re-glob cadence - T5 in I8 measures it on the box. If the agent
turned out to glob only once at startup, the gap would be permanent for containers created after
the agent started, and the fix would additionally need `ExecStartPost` chaining. T5 exists to
discover that.

**8. Concurrency.** `Type=oneshot` plus systemd's per-unit job serialisation means two invocations
cannot overlap; a start requested while one is running is queued or coalesced. Two concurrent
`setfacl -R` runs would in any case be idempotent and convergent.

**9. Startup/shutdown ordering.** The `.service` carries `After=docker.service` so a boot-time run
cannot race the daemon creating the directory; and the script's `[ -d "$DIR" ] || exit 0` guard
makes an early run a clean no-op rather than an error. `OnBootSec=2min` gives docker time to come
up before the first timed run.

**10. A partially applied fix.** Each of the three grants is independent: group membership alone
fixes six entries; the letsencrypt `chmod` alone fixes the seventh; the reconciler alone fixes the
eighth. There is no ordering dependency between them and no state one leaves that another needs.
A partial application degrades to "fewer log groups populated", never to a broken box.

**11. Does any of this touch the application?** No. Nothing in `backend/`, `frontend/`, the engine,
the SSE transport, the run queues, or the database is read or written. An unattached client, a slow
client, a crashed run, a restart, a resume, a fan-out run, a revision run, two browsers - all
unaffected by construction, because no application code path exists in the change. Memory and
connection-pool effects: none (the change adds one short-lived root process per minute).

**12. The one interaction with a sibling issue that could bite.** If B1 has **not** landed, the
agent is still crash-looping on `/var/log/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.log` and `systemctl restart
amazon-cloudwatch-agent` in step 4 will restart a process that immediately exits 1 again. B2's own
verification (T2/T3) would then be unrunnable. That is a sequencing constraint, not a defect - see
I10.
